evaluation.positioning_hook: A sleep-deprived boarding-school student uncovers a dorm room that erases students from memory every eleven years — and learns the only way to save his friend may be to vanish himself.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to sell in one sentence and sits in a proven horror-thriller lane with a clean emotional spine: save the friend, survive the room, keep your name. The boarding-school setting and the 1:11 motif give it a recognizable hook that can travel well with genre audiences.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script establishes the engine quickly: a dorm, a missing student, a repeating 11-year pattern, and a room that seems to take names. The notebook, yearbook pattern, and James Walker reveal all sharpen the central mystery into something a casual viewer can track.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ryan has a usable internal contradiction — he wants to matter but behaves like someone already half-erased — and James Walker gives the story a memorable antagonist voice. Rhea adds emotional texture, though the script mostly uses her as the human counterweight to Ryan’s investigation rather than giving her a fully separate engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The idea of a room feeding on social disappearance, not just physical death, gives the horror a fresh psychological angle. The 1:11 clock, the eleven-year cycle, and the notebook/yearbook mechanics make the mythology feel authored rather than generic.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The mystery keeps turning over with new clues, and the final confrontation in Room 111 delivers a clear payoff. The middle section spends a fair amount of time in observational dorm-life passages and repeated hallway beats, which gives the script atmosphere more than forward pressure.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script lands on a strong, inevitable-feeling idea: students don’t just disappear, they get socially edited out of existence. That combination of supernatural horror and adolescent invisibility feels immediately legible and emotionally specific.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The dorm-school environment has useful rules — roll call, curfew, sign-out desks, mailboxes, yearbooks — and those details help the mystery feel lived-in. The world is still primarily a container for the central haunting rather than a fully layered institutional ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends quiet teen alienation, procedural clue-hunting, and ghost-story dread in a way that feels coherent. The voiceover about sleep deprivation and social invisibility gives the script a reflective, haunted quality that distinguishes it from a standard haunted-house setup.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the horror engine is a clear thematic layer about being unseen, performing normalcy, and the emotional cost of disappearing into routine. The ending, with Rhea’s note and the final Room 111 selection, suggests the mythology can keep opening outward.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ryan and Rhea carry the emotional center, and James gives the story a strong opposing force, but most other characters function as gatekeepers or witnesses. The script has enough relationship energy for the feature, though it is not built as a broad ensemble engine.

casting_characteristics: One principal male antagonist with a strong physical silhouette

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical atmosphere with selective shadow/mirror effects, flickering lights, and a final selection/title-card style visual beat.
technical.sfx_needs: Door movement, light flicker, blood-smeared key, practical darkness and sound design-driven scares.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a festival-to-platform or genre-platform title.

cost.note: Contemporary, mostly contained to dorm interiors and school spaces, with minor effects and no large-scale set pieces.

cast.note: A small teen/young adult cast centered on Ryan, Rhea, and James keeps the casting footprint manageable.

location.note: The story lives in a compact set of recurring locations: dorm hallways, rooms, office, classroom, and a few nearby public spaces.

content.note: The horror is driven by dread, disappearance, and a few bloody details, with language and psychological pressure rather than explicit gore.

rights.note: No named music, brands, or real-person references appear to drive the story.

whats_special.headline: ROOM 111 has a clean, marketable horror engine: a boarding-school dorm room that erases students from existence unless someone is willing to take their place. The script pairs that concept with a strong emotional undercurrent about loneliness, social invisibility, and the terror of realizing you’ve already started disappearing.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.hook: Ryan is a sleep-deprived boarding-school kid who moves through life like he’s already half out of frame. He’s observant, emotionally guarded, and quietly aching to matter, which makes him both the story’s investigator and its most vulnerable target.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Justice Smith in *The Get Down* or Jaeden Martell in *It* — a young lead whose stillness, anxiety, and buried feeling become the engine of the performance. Actors will want the chance to play a character who starts as an internalized observer and ends up carrying a full emotional breakdown, survival drive, and moral choice in one role.

lead_characters.name: Rhea
lead_characters.hook: Rhea is the emotionally intuitive counterpoint to Ryan: present enough to notice what’s wrong, but drifting enough to recognize herself in the story’s theme of being overlooked. She has warmth, guardedness, and a lived-in sadness that gives the movie its human pulse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Auliʻi Cravalho in *The Power* or Rachel Zegler in *West Side Story* — a role that lets an actor carry tenderness, romantic tension, and a dawning sense of dread without losing naturalism. Young actresses looking for a part that can play intimacy, fear, and emotional recognition in the same frame will chase this.

lead_characters.name: James Walker
lead_characters.hook: James Walker is the room’s resident ghost with a human face: elegant, controlled, and unnervingly calm, with a predator’s patience and a philosopher’s language. He feels like someone who has spent years turning isolation into doctrine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal villain role that gave Ralph Fiennes in *The Menu* or Matthew McConaughey in *True Detective* their scene-commanding showcase space — a character whose intelligence and menace arrive together. Character actors and prestige genre leads will want the monologue territory, the age-defying mystery, and the chance to make the antagonist feel seductive before he turns terrifying.

lead_characters.name: Mrs. Wesman
lead_characters.hook: Mrs. Wesman is the office authority who keeps the dorm machine running while never quite seeing how strange it has become. She reads as practical, distracted, and institutionally trained to smooth over anything that threatens routine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded authority role that gives an actor the same functional texture as Frances McDormand in *Fargo* or Patricia Clarkson in *Sharp Objects* — a seemingly ordinary adult whose calm becomes ominous by proximity. Experienced character actors will like the chance to play institutional denial with just enough warmth to keep the audience unsure.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Brusco
lead_characters.hook: Mr. Brusco is the dorm enforcer who floats between joke, warning, and gatekeeper. He has the kind of casual authority that makes him feel harmless right up until the room starts bending around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of supporting authority part that lets an actor do the dry, unsettling utility work seen in *The Leftovers* or *The OA* — a character who can land exposition while still feeling like part of the mystery. Character actors who specialize in ambiguous institutional figures will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Henzy
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Henzy is the softer adult presence in the school, the one who makes the place feel normal until the normality itself starts to feel haunted. She’s lightly comic, lightly maternal, and useful as a reminder that the system keeps moving even when people vanish.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small but memorable role that gives an actor the same lived-in utility as a teacher or counselor in *Eighth Grade* or *The Holdovers* — a part that can ground the world with a few precise beats. Supporting players who like to make a room feel real with minimal screen time will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Jeff
lead_characters.hook: Jeff is the comic-pressure valve of the dorm, the guy who keeps showing up at the edge of the mystery with snacks, bad timing, and casual social noise. He makes the school feel populated, which is exactly why his presence matters.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing teen supporting role that works like the friend parts in *Booksmart* or *The Breakfast Club* — a character who can bring levity while still living inside the same haunted social ecosystem. Young actors who want a memorable supporting turn with personality and rhythm will gravitate toward it.

lead_characters.name: Roommate
lead_characters.hook: Rhea’s roommate is a quiet witness with just enough perspective to sharpen Rhea’s emotional state. She functions like the script’s private mirror, catching what Rhea won’t say out loud.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of intimate supporting role that gives an actor the same conversational, revealing space as the roommate/friend parts in *Lady Bird* or *Euphoria* — a scene partner who can land emotional truth without needing a large arc. Actors who excel at naturalistic dialogue and subtle reaction work will see the value immediately.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make dread out of routine.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with a strong short-film reel in psychological horror, elevated thriller, or contained genre drama. This material rewards precision, atmosphere, and performance-forward tension more than spectacle, so it fits filmmakers who already think in terms of hallway geometry, sound design, and emotional unease.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a contained playground where lighting, blocking, and silence can do as much work as the mythology. It will appeal to directors who like genre stories that stay intimate while still landing a clean, high-concept payoff.

buyer_appeal.detail: The cast can be anchored by three young leads and a handful of adult support roles, so it does not require a heavy-name ensemble to function. The contained dorm-and-school footprint and minor effects package make it a natural fit for buyers looking for a low-to-mid budget horror title with a clean hook and exportable premise.

considerations.area: The middle leans atmospheric before the mythology locks.
considerations.detail: The dorm-life passages, hallway repetition, and voiceover sections build mood effectively, and the version of the script where one or two of those beats are folded into the clue trail would keep the mystery charging forward. The strongest lever is to let each observational passage also move the investigation one step, so the atmosphere and the engine arrive together.

considerations.area: Rhea’s final note can carry more setup.
considerations.detail: The ending lands emotionally because it reframes her as someone who has been disappearing in plain sight, and a next pass could seed that emotional state earlier in her scenes with Ryan. That would make the final note feel less like a reveal and more like the inevitable emotional destination of the relationship.

considerations.area: The Room 111 rules are clear, but one clean line could sharpen them.
considerations.detail: The notebook, the eleven-year cycle, and the name-erasure logic all track, and the version of the confrontation where James states the transfer mechanism in one distilled sentence would make the mythology even easier to carry in marketing and audience memory. This is a small clarity pass, not a structural change.

The script already lives in a practical, shootable lane, so the main simplification lever is protecting the recurring dorm locations and avoiding any expansion beyond the school ecosystem. Keeping the story inside the dorm, classroom, office, café, and library spaces preserves the feature’s atmosphere while protecting budget.
